_readme: MONEY-979 — the SECOND monitor template in this directory, and the reason a
monitor-zero-write.json can express exactly one question: 'work was selected
and none was written'. It is a `query alert` over two COUNTERS with
thresholds.critical fixed at 0 and a clamp_max difference. No substitution of
its placeholders can turn that into a percentile over a latency series — the
metric type, the query shape and the threshold semantics all differ. (It said
'a percentile over a DISTRIBUTION' until the MONEY-979 review; the series is a
histogram, and that word being wrong here is where the broken query came
The gate this serves is MONEY-979's: filing -> stored, p95 under 5 minutes.
The series is a HISTOGRAM (stockbook.edgar.detect_latency_seconds), emitted
once per newly-detected filing as now - acceptedAt. acceptedAt, not filedAt:
a filing accepted 21:53 ET is DATED the next business day, so a latency built
on filedAt would be NEGATIVE most evenings.
_query_form_rationale: THE QUERY FORM IS DECIDED BY THE WIRE TYPE, and this line got it wrong for
one release. It read:
percentile(last_1h):p95:stockbook.edgar.detect_latency_seconds{...}
`percentile(...)` / `p95:` is the DISTRIBUTION query form. outcome.py emits
`statsd.histogram(...)`, whose wire packet is
`…detect_latency_seconds:12.5|h|` — DogStatsD type `h`. The Agent aggregates
a histogram CLIENT-SIDE into sub-metrics (`.avg`, `.count`, `.median`,
`.max`, and `.95percentile` from the default `histogram_percentiles`) and
ships those; the BASE name is never a percentile-queryable series. So the
monitor watched a series that cannot exist — and the `_readme` two keys up
SAID 'the series is a HISTOGRAM' while the query below it asked Datadog for
a distribution. Both halves were in this file, disagreeing, in view.
Two repairs were possible. This file takes (a):
(a) KEEP the histogram, query the Agent's `.95percentile` sub-metric.
A pure query change, in this file, verifiable by rendering it.
(b) SWITCH the emit to `statsd.distribution(...)` and keep `percentile()`.
(a), for four reasons, in the order they weigh:
1. IT IS THE HOUSE CONVENTION. packages/datadog/src/metrics.ts exports
exactly `increment`, `gauge` and `histogram` — there is no
`distribution` in the TypeScript metrics surface at all, and no
first-party `statsd.distribution` / `metrics.distribution` call exists
anywhere in this repo. (b) would make the ONE distribution metric we
own live on the Python side of a two-language seam, with no TS
counterpart to keep it honest.
2. (b) DOES NOT FIX THE QUERY BY ITSELF. A DogStatsD distribution reaches
Datadog as a distribution, but `p95:` resolves against it only once
PERCENTILE AGGREGATION has been enabled for that metric in the org
(Metrics -> Manage percentile aggregations, or the metric tag-config
API). Nothing in this repo provisions that and nothing here can verify
it. That is the same objection `_notify_no_data_rationale` makes
against options.scheduling.custom_schedule — and it is worse here,
because the result is a query that LOOKS fixed and still resolves to
nothing until somebody remembers to click something.
3. (b) CHANGES THE WIRE TYPE AND THE AGENT'S REQUIREMENTS — `|h|` becomes
`|d|`, aggregation moves from the Agent to the intake, and the metric
is billed as a distribution. That is a deployment change dressed as a
one-word edit.
4. (b) BREAKS THE EMITTER'S OWN TESTS: test_detect_job.py asserts
`kind == "histogram"` at two sites.
WHAT (a) COSTS, written down rather than discovered later: `.95percentile`
is computed PER AGENT, so with more than one instance reporting there is no
true global p95 to query — only a set of per-instance p95s that a space
aggregator must collapse. `max:` is the choice here: any single instance
breaching the gate pages, which is the conservative reading for a latency
SLO. `avg:` would dilute one bad instance against the healthy ones and is
the wrong error to prefer for an alarm. Should this ever need a true global
percentile across instances, that is the argument for (b) — and it comes
WITH the percentile-aggregation provisioning step, not instead of it.
packages/datadog/__tests__/monitor-agreement.test.ts now checks the class
rather than this instance: it reads the EMIT TYPE of every metric a rendered
monitor names, out of the Python and TypeScript that emit it, and fails when
the query FORM does not match. A name check alone cannot see this defect —
the name was right the whole time.
_notify_routing_rationale: The message ends `@{{notify}}`, and the `@` is the entire mechanism. It read
`{{notify}}` for one release, which renders as
…edgar-engine.md\ndeepshaswat@gmail.com
— Datadog routes on an `@handle` DIRECTIVE inside the message body, so a
bare handle is just text. The monitor triggered and notified NOBODY. The
sibling monitor-zero-write.json has always ended `@{{notify}}`; this
template dropped the one character that does the work.
WHAT MAKES IT WORTH A NAMED KEY is what it stacked with. Until MONEY-979's
review round this monitor had THREE independent defects, and each one alone
would have been survivable:
1. the query asked for a percentile of a histogram's base name, so it
watched a series that cannot exist (see _query_form_rationale)
2. `notify_no_data: false` — deliberate and still correct, but it means
the emptiness in (1) could never announce itself
3. this missing `@` — so even a breach that DID evaluate routed nowhere
Composed: it could not page on breach, could not page on absence, and
probably had no series to evaluate. A monitor in that state is
indistinguishable from a healthy one from the outside, which is precisely
the shape MONEY-1220 built this directory to stop shipping.
monitor-agreement.test.ts asserts that every occurrence of the notify handle
in EVERY rendered monitor's message is immediately preceded by `@`, so a
third template cannot repeat it.
name: [{{env}}] {{job}} — p95 latency over {{threshold_seconds}}s
message:
{{job}}: p95 of {{metric}} exceeded {{threshold_seconds}}s over the last {{window}}.

This measures filing acceptance at SEC to the row landing in Mongo. A rise means one of: the detection loop is behind (check the getcurrent walk's page count and whether it is hitting its 20-page cap at the 16:00-18:00 ET peak), the shared 9 req/s Redis budget is saturated, or a parser is slow enough to back up its subscription.

_managed_tag_rationale: `managed-by:apply-monitors` is LOAD-BEARING and was missing from this
template while the zero-write one carried it. apply-monitors.sh finds the
monitor it is about to update with ONE listing —
on the rendered name inside it. Without the tag this monitor is never in
that listing, so `EXISTING_ID` is empty on every run and every run POSTs a
NEW one: two monitors after the second run, three after the third, each
alerting independently. That is MONEY-1238's fault (e) verbatim, in the
template added by the ticket that cites it.
monitor-agreement.test.ts could not catch it. Its stub answers the listing
with RENDERED_PROD — both templates — so the latency monitor is present in
the test's listing and absent from the real one. The stub is generous where
_notify_no_data_rationale: notify_no_data is FALSE here, and it is the ONE option on which this
template deliberately disagrees with monitor-zero-write.json. It read TRUE
for one release, with the argument that 'a detection loop that stops
emitting is indistinguishable from a market with no filings unless silence
itself pages, and no filings at all is never true on a US weekday'. The
premise is correct. The conclusion did not follow, and the monitor paged in
two states we ship on purpose:
BEFORE THE FIRST FILING. This series is emitted at ONE site — detect.py's
fan-out, only for a filing that was newly claim_filing-ed. Prod now ships
EDGAR_DETECT="on", so points DO arrive — but only once the service is
deployed, the seven push subscriptions exist and SEC publishes something.
This monitor is created in the runbook's FIRST-DEPLOY block, ahead of all
three, so no_data_timeframe would expire and page against a service
behaving exactly as designed.
(This clause read differently for one release: EDGAR_DETECT shipped
"off", so the argument was zero points until a separate arming step
hours to weeks later. The engine now ships ARMED and that leg is gone.
The conclusion is unchanged because the weekend case below never
depended on it — recorded rather than quietly rewritten, because a
rationale whose premise has gone stale is how a setting outlives its
reason.)
EVERY WEEKEND, EVEN FULLY ARMED. SEC accepts filings on business days, so
Saturday 00:00 ET -> Monday 06:00 ET is ~54h with no sample. Monitors
evaluate on weekends; 'never true on a US WEEKDAY' says nothing about the
other two days. That is the same muted-alarm shape apply-monitors.sh
argues at length for the five event-driven edgar-parse-* jobs, and the
same one that got bhavcopy-sync's 36h-on-a-1-5-cron muted in MONEY-1238.
SILENCE IS STILL WATCHED, by the instrument that can actually see it.
'Detection produced nothing' is a zero-write question, and edgar-detect has
a zero-write monitor: apply-monitors.sh's MONITORED_JOBS carries
`edgar-detect|6h|every 1 min (atom) + hourly EFTS reconcile, all days`, with
notify_no_data TRUE and an 18h no-data window. That one CAN hold the line
where this one cannot, because its series is fed from a different place:
detect.py calls report_job_outcome from a `finally` that wraps the flag
check itself, so every one of the 1,440 daily runs emits selected/written —
disarmed, armed, weekday, weekend, holiday. A quiet run emits 0/0, which the
clamped difference reads as healthy, and NO DATA there can only mean the
scheduler or the service stopped. Which is exactly what should page.
So the split is: THIS monitor answers 'is detection SLOW', the zero-write
monitor answers 'is detection THERE'. Do not restore notify_no_data here to
recover coverage — there is none to recover, and doing so re-arms both
false-page paths above.
options.scheduling.custom_schedule (evaluate only inside US business hours)
was considered as the alternative and NOT used. It would fix the weekend
case and not the disarmed one, and it is an option this repo cannot verify
without a live Datadog call — shipping an unverified option in the script
whose worst failure is a monitor that never applies buys a 400 for a
problem already solved by one boolean.
no_data_timeframe STAYS, and is inert rather than vestigial: apply-monitors.sh's
render() coerces options.no_data_timeframe to a Number unconditionally for
both templates, so deleting the key here renders `"no_data_timeframe": null`
— a null where Datadog expects an integer. It is the window that WOULD apply
if a later change re-enables notification, and it costs nothing while false.
_new_group_delay_removed: REMOVED. Datadog answers 400 "The new_group_delay option can only be used for multi-alert monitors" - this is a simple alert with no group-by, so it has no groups to delay. Measured on the first live apply.
